questions.q: Why does the lesson say to complete the offer worksheet before writing any campaign copy?
options: Because AI can't write copy until a full price list exists
Because email rules require the offer to be documented first
Because even great copy can't rescue a weak offer
Because the worksheet replaces the need for a human review
questions.explain: The lesson's first principle is to start with the offer, not the copy, because great copy can't rescue a weak offer; AI can then help pressure-test it.

questions.q: A yoga studio's AI-drafted ad reads: 'Struggling with back pain? Join our class.' What's the problem, according to the lesson?
options: It's too short to meet the platform's minimum length for ads
It doesn't include a guarantee of results for new members
It uses the problem angle instead of the outcome angle
It implies the viewer's health condition, which platforms reject
questions.explain: The lesson's ad rules forbid wording that asserts or implies the viewer's personal characteristics, and notes that major ad platforms reject ads that call out sensitive attributes such as health.

questions.q: A solo bookkeeper's AI-drafted 'last call' email says only five spots remain, but she has no real limit. What should she do before sending?
options: Remove the false scarcity, since deadlines and limits must be real
Keep it, since urgency is a normal part of any last-call email
Ask AI to soften the wording so the limit sounds less certain
Send it now, then review it with fresh eyes the next morning
questions.explain: The lesson's review checklist requires scarcity to be real, and the last-call email belongs in a sequence only if there's a real deadline.
